title: So Protestants do not deny a remote and imperfect power in man before grace
source_text: XLVII. Porro ex iis quae hactenus exposita sunt patet Protestantes non negare, post peccatum & ante gratiam, homini inesse potentiam quandam remotam & imperfectam ad opera pietatis & supernaturalia. Et hoc nomine illos designare facultatem naturalem volendi & nolendi, quae respectu istorum operum proportionem quandam & capacitatem homini conciliat, qualis nec in lapidibus, nec in brutis reperitur.
pass_a_gloss: XLVII. Further from those things which have so far been set out it is plain that the Protestants do not deny that, after sin and before grace, there is in man a certain remote and imperfect power for the works of piety and supernatural ones. And that by this name they designate the natural faculty of willing and nilling, which in respect of those works procures for man a certain proportion and capacity, such as is found neither in stones, nor in brutes.
pass_b_english: What has been set out so far shows that the Protestants do not deny that after sin and before grace man has a remote and imperfect power for works of piety and supernatural works.
By that name they mean the natural faculty of willing and refusing, which gives man a certain proportion to such works and capacity for them, of a kind found neither in stones nor in beasts.
